title: Lençóis Maranhenses National Park, Brazil
caption: Info
subtitle: Lençóis Maranhenses National Park, Brazil
description:
Think you know what a desert looks like? Lençóis Maranhenses National Park might change your mind. Along Brazil's Maranhão coast, huge white dunes sit beside freshwater lagoons, creating a landscape that changes with the seasons. Established as a national park in 1981 and recognised as a UNESCO World Heritage Site in 2024, it covers more than 156,000 hectares (about 386,887 acres) and stretches along 80 kilometres of coastline. The dunes are shaped by prevailing winds, while seasonal rains collect in the hollows between them. Some lagoons last only through the wet season, while others remain year-round, including Lagoa da Esperança.
The Lençóis Maranhenses National Park also includes beaches, mangroves and restinga vegetation, with connections to the Cerrado, Caatinga and Amazon biomes. From Barreirinhas, visitors can take guided 4x4 tours to lagoons such as Lagoa Azul and Lagoa Bonita. Beyond its striking scenery, the park supports plants and wildlife adapted to an environment shaped by both sand and seasonal water.

title: Eiffel Tower at sunset, Paris, France
caption: Info
subtitle: Eiffel Tower at sunset, Paris, France
description:
No other city is nearly as romanticised as Paris. Yet the French capital's history has not always been as rosy as the sunset glowing behind the Eiffel Tower. Built for the 1889 Exposition Universelle, or the World's Fair, which marked the centennial of the start of the French Revolution, the tower was originally intended to serve as the fair's entrance centrepiece. Designed by engineer Gustave Eiffel and his team, the iron landmark rose 300 metres above the Champ de Mars and became the tallest structure in the world at the time.
Many locals criticised the bold design, but it quickly captured the public's imagination. During the World's Fair, millions came to see the monument and enjoy panoramic views unlike any they had experienced before.
Today, visitors can stroll along the Seine and explore old neighbourhoods and museums throughout a city that continues to reinvent itself. As evening falls and the Eiffel Tower glows against the night sky, it remains a powerful symbol of French creativity, ambition and resilience.

title: Sea otter grooming fur, Monterey Bay, California, United States
caption: Info
subtitle: Sea otter grooming fur, Monterey Bay, California, United States
description:
Few animals are as closely tied to the health of coastal ecosystems as the sea otter. In today's image, one grooms its fur in Monterey Bay, California, USA. This behaviour is far more than a daily ritual. Unlike seals and whales, sea otters have little insulating blubber, so they rely on the densest fur of any animal. Careful cleaning traps air within their coat, creating a waterproof layer that helps them stay warm in the cold Pacific.
Sea otters are also considered a keystone species. By feeding on sea urchins and other invertebrates, they help control populations that can otherwise overgraze kelp forests. Their foraging habits are equally fascinating: they are among the few marine mammals known to use tools, often cracking open shellfish with stones. When resting, they may wrap themselves in kelp to avoid drifting away, while mothers keep pups close on their chests as they float. Protection from hunting has allowed some populations to recover, although sea otters still face threats from disease, food shortages, pollution and shark bites.

title: Autumn aspen trees near Guardsman Pass, Utah, United States
caption: Info
subtitle: Autumn aspen trees near Guardsman Pass, Utah, United States
description:
What makes a tree 'quake?' Take a closer look at an aspen leaf. Its flattened stalk catches even a light breeze, making the leaves flutter and giving the tree its name: quaking aspen. Near Guardsman Pass in Utah, United States, these trees form striking groves across the higher mountain slopes, where cooler, moist conditions suit them well.
Quaking aspen is Utah's state tree and one of the state's most common forest types. It grows mainly at higher elevations, often alongside spruce and fir, and spreads through root sprouts. This means a grove can contain many stems connected to one root system, forming a genetically identical clone. In autumn, the leaves turn shades of yellow and orange before falling.
Aspen has practical uses too. Its light, soft wood is used for lumber, pallets, crates, pulp and matches. The trees also provide food and shelter for wildlife, protect soils and watersheds and offer forage for animals such as elk and deer. At Guardsman Pass, their seasonal colour is a reminder that these trees are useful long after the leaves have changed.

title: Hobbit house at Hobbiton Movie Set, Matamata, New Zealand
caption: Info
subtitle: Hobbit house at Hobbiton Movie Set, Matamata, New Zealand
description:
A round door, a bright green frame and a hillside that looks straight out of Middle-earth—welcome to Hobbiton Movie Set in Matamata, New Zealand. Built in 1999 for 'The Lord of the Rings,' the original set featured 39 temporary Hobbit Holes across a 4.9-hectare site. After filming ended, the set was dismantled, but it returned in 2009 for 'The Hobbit' films and was rebuilt as a permanent attraction.
The Hobbit house pictured here is one of the detailed Hobbit Holes that bring the Shire to life. Each one was designed with its own character, from colourful gardens and tiny pathways to distinctive round doors. Bag End, the home of Bilbo and Frodo Baggins, sits above the Party Tree and is among the set's best-known spots. Today, Hobbiton has 44 permanent Hobbit Holes, and visitors can step inside a recreated Hobbit home on Bagshot Row. One thing is certain: Middle-earth has never looked quite so inviting.

title: Castelmezzano, Basilicata, Italy
caption: Info
subtitle: Castelmezzano, Basilicata, Italy
description:
Castelmezzano, in the province of Potenza in Basilicata, Italy, is hidden from view until you reach it. You arrive through a tunnel and as you emerge, the village suddenly appears, wedged among the sandstone pinnacles of the Lucanian Dolomites. The houses seem to climb over one another at around 750 metres above sea level, connected by steps and narrow lanes that rise towards the remains of the Norman fortress.
The name Castelmezzano comes from Castrum Medianum, meaning 'castle in the middle,' referring to its position between the fortresses of nearby Pietrapertosa and Brindisi Montagna. A steep staircase carved into the rock leads to the former lookout point, with views over the Basento Valley below. The village has around 700 residents and is part of I Borghi più belli d'Italia, a network of Italy's most beautiful villages. It is also one of the two stations of the Volo dell'Angelo (Angel's Flight), a steel-cable zip line linking Castelmezzano and Pietrapertosa, with riders suspended high above the valley. A village to admire from below and, if you're feeling brave, from above too.

title: Jog Falls, Sharavathi River, Karnataka, India
caption: Info
subtitle: Jog Falls, Karnataka, India
description:
Most rivers spend their lives flowing around obstacles. The Sharavathi River reaches the edge of a cliff and simply jumps. At Jog Falls in Karnataka, the river plunges 253 metres, making it the third-highest waterfall in India.
Set in the Western Ghats, Jog Falls is formed by four distinct cascades: Raja, Rani, Roarer and Rocket. Each stream has its own style before joining the grand plunge below. Raja descends with royal composure, Roarer provides the soundtrack, Rocket lives up to its name and Rani adds a touch of grace.
The falls are at their most powerful during the monsoon, when water surges over the cliffs in a curtain of white. In drier months, the separate streams become easier to spot. Either way, visitors are treated to a view that makes quite a splash. At Jog Falls, the river's biggest drop is also its biggest moment.

title: Cedar Mesa and Muley Point near Bears Ears National Monument, Utah, United States
caption: Info
description: What do a bear's ears, a house on fire and a road packed with hairpin turns have in common? They're all part of the story of America's public lands in southeastern Utah. Bears Ears National Monument protects important cultural and natural resources, including archaeological sites that reflect thousands of years of human history. Its name comes from two buttes that rise side by side and resemble a bear's ears.
